title: A Variable-Angle-Distance Quantum Evolutionary Algorithm for 2D HP Model
journal_or_venue: ICCCS 2018 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, LNCS 11068)
abstract_summary: This paper proposes QEA-VAR, a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm that uses a variable angle-distance rotation strategy to solve the NP-hard 2D hydrophobic-polar (HP) protein folding model. By leveraging quantum representations and an adaptive rotation update, QEA-VAR improves convergence speed and robustness versus standard evolutionary methods and obtains lower-energy conformations on benchmark sequences. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm's superior efficiency and effectiveness compared to differential evolution and particle swarm optimization. This paper studies the relationship between web news topic intensity evolution and topic content evolution. Using a time pre-discretized LDA topic extraction followed by K-means clustering, the authors apply a topic-content evolution model (creation, split, drift, keep, merge, end) and propose a method to quantify topic content and intensity. Experiments on social news datasets show a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.74) and a >71.5% likelihood that topic intensity and content complexity increase or decrease together. This paper addresses the NP-hard problem of forming a cooperative team in a social network to satisfy a set of required skills while minimizing intra-team communication cost. The authors adapt the Imperialist Competitive Algorithm (ICA) to a discrete team-formation setting by introducing genetic-style operators, imperialist mutation, and an imperialist crossover with similarity detection, and demonstrate on a DBLP-derived dataset that the approach yields high-quality teams under different communication-cost measures (diameter and sum-of-distances) compared to several state-of-the-art baselines.
methodology_description: This paper proposes CWDR-BiGRU, a bilingual word embedding training and transfer-learning pipeline designed for low-resource languages. The approach first pre-trains bilingual embeddings via a modified Skip-gram style objective using a novel Cross-Context Window of Dynamic Ratio (CWDR) that interleaves words from aligned sentence pairs according to their length ratios, producing mixed-context sentences that serve as additional cross-lingual training contexts. This pre-training preserves monolingual objectives while adding cross-lingual constraints. Next, pre-trained embeddings are further updated by an encoder–decoder based on a bidirectional GRU (BiGRU) with an attention mechanism, which learns contextual alignment between source and target words and refines embeddings. The resulting bilingual embeddings (same vector space) are then used for downstream transfer tasks: training a model on labeled data in a high-resource language and applying it directly to low-resource language samples (no labeled data required there). Evaluation includes qualitative semantic reasoning and t-SNE visualization, and quantitative cross-lingual document classification accuracy comparisons against several baselines. This study investigates the relationship between web-news topic intensity evolution and topic content evolution. The authors first segment a time-stamped news text corpus into time-slices and extract latent topics within each slice using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Topics are represented by their top words and treated as low-dimensional representations; topics across slices are clustered using K-means with a relative-entropy based similarity measure for topic-to-topic matching. A formal topic-content evolution model is applied to detect six basic evolutionary states (creation, split, drift, keep, merge, end) between topics in adjacent slices; two thresholds (r and e, with r<e) are used to classify the state based on inter-topic similarities. These thresholds are chosen via grid search (coarse then fine) over held-out data, yielding r = 0.20 and e = 0.38 for the authors' experiments. Topic-content complexity is quantiﬁed by measuring changes in content across slices (using the described similarity / split/merge criteria and the derived K slopes from a multi-scale box-counting–style analysis); topic intensity is quantified per topic via a separate time-pre-discretized measure (based on counts/weights of articles per topic per slice). Finally, the relationship between topic-content complexity time series and topic-intensity time series is assessed using Pearson correlation and percent-synchronous-change statistics, reporting a mean Pearson r of 0.74 and ~71.5% chance of simultaneous increase/decrease. In addition, the authors employ gray relational analysis (GRA) to relate extracted feature vectors to known topic labels when constructing a knowledge base for further analysis. The paper proposes a discriminative sparse representation framework for face recognition under occlusion. Deep features are first extracted using a CNN trained with a center-loss-style supervision to learn discriminative feature embeddings for each class. A class-specific dictionary D = [D1, D2, ..., DK] is then learned along with sparse codes Z and a linear classiﬁer W by minimizing an objective composed of: (i) a reconstruction term ||A - D Z||_F^2, (ii) an L1 sparsity term on Z, (iii) a representation-constrained term that penalizes deviations of class coefﬁcient blocks from their class means (||Z - m||_F^2), (iv) a classiﬁcation error term ||W Z - B||_F^2 (B are one-hot labels) and (v) a coefﬁcient incoherence regularizer ||W||_F^2. The optimization is carried out by alternating minimization: when D and W are fixed, Z is updated (closed-form linear system with L1 sparsity handled via standard sparse coding); when Z and W are fixed, D is updated via Lagrange dual methods with column normalization constraints; when D and Z are fixed, W is updated by least squares (closed form). The authors report experiments on two face benchmarks with occlusion (AR and CAS-PEAL), using single neutral training images per identity and testing on occluded variants (sunglasses, scarf, hats). Performance is compared against SRC, RSC, CESR and ESRC using recognition accuracy as the primary metric.

results_summary: The paper introduces QEA-VAR, a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm that uses a variable angle-distance quantum rotation operator to update quantum-like representations for 2D HP protein folding. On a set of standard benchmark sequences (lengths 20–85) QEA-VAR consistently outperformed a differential evolution baseline and a particle swarm optimizer in terms of convergence speed and the average minimum energy found over repeated runs. For many moderate-length instances (≤50) QEA-VAR found the published optimal energy every run; for larger instances (60, 64, 85) it found the best-known minima many times (e.g., 20/25 runs) and attained superior average energies. The authors conclude that the variable-angle-distance strategy improves search eﬃciency and robustness against local optima. This work proposes multilevel feature fusion strategies (accumulation, concatenation, weighted concatenation) that combine intermediate pooling-layer outputs with the network's final representation for image-classification. Implemented in several VGG-like variants and a 6-layer MP-net, the fusion schemes consistently improved CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 accuracy versus plain VGG-like baselines. Weighted concatenation (VGG-Fw) produced the strongest results: e.g., 93.39% on CIFAR-10 with augmentation and 72.19% on CIFAR-100 with augmentation. Experiments also indicate that increasing depth further improves performance and that the fusion approach can yield competitive accuracy while being computationally efficient. The supplied conference-paper material does not contain any studies or statements about quantum computing in financial services. Instead, the text comprises multiple unrelated conference papers: a study of topic intensity evolution of web news (LDA, K-means, topic-content evolution and correlation with intensity), a team-formation approach in social networks using the Imperialist Competitive Algorithm, CST-based lightning-strike simulation for ships, and a discriminative dictionary-learning method for face recognition with occlusion. No experiments, metrics, or theoretical analyses pertaining to quantum algorithms, quantum hardware, portfolio optimization, risk analysis, or other finance-related quantum applications are present in the provided text.
